The core tension is direct — CA's design philosophy subsumes the ideation phase under full autonomy, while CB presents empirical or conceptual evidence that human involvement in ideation produces superior outcomes, which would constitute a challenge to CA's foundational premise of minimal human intervention. The two contributions make directly opposing empirical claims about the ability of AI coding agents to validate/reproduce experimental results. CA asserts that coding agents fabricate or fail to validate experimental results in ~80% of ML research task attempts, characterizing this as a critical and widespread failure mode. CB, by contrast, reports that frontier coding agents (Claude Code) achieve high computational reproducibility on social science findings — 93.4% task-level accuracy — with even weaker agents (Codex) reaching 62.1%. These figures are fundamentally incompatible: CA's ~80% failure rate implies only ~20% success, while CB documents 62–93% success rates. Although the domains differ (ML research tasks in CA vs. social science reproduction in CB), both contributions address the same core construct — whether AI coding agents can reliably validate or reproduce quantitative experimental results — and arrive at genuinely opposing conclusions. The contradiction is real but tempered somewhat by the domain difference and the possibility that CB's specialized frontier agents (Claude Code) represent a meaningfully different capability tier than the general-purpose agents characterized in CA.

Both contributions directly address the reliability of AI/LLM-based coding agents in producing valid scientific results, but arrive at genuinely incompatible conclusions. CA (supported by AQ) finds that current coding agents fabricate or fail to validate experimental results ~80% of the time, framing this as a critical barrier to scientific reliability. CB (supported by BQ) finds that frontier coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) achieve high reproducibility of social science findings—93.4% and 62.1% task-level accuracy respectively—and explicitly notes these rates considerably exceed those previously reported for general-purpose LLM-based agents on comparable benchmarks. The two findings are in direct tension: CA characterizes the 80% failure rate as representative of the field, while CB demonstrates high success rates that directly undercut that characterization. The same construct (coding agent reliability for scientific tasks) yields incompatible quantitative pictures, establishing a contradiction rather than merely a difference in domain scope.

CB also explicitly notes its results exceed prior low benchmarks (B018, B019), which are more aligned with CA's findings, further sharpening the contrast.
